6.0.0.en: 1 Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came! 2 Pass ye unto Calneh, and see; and from thence go ye to Hamath the great: then go down to Gath of the Philistines: be they better than these kingdoms? or their border greater than your border? 3 Ye that put far away the evil day, and cause the seat of violence to come near; 4 That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall; 5 That chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David; 6 That drink wine in bowls, and anoint themselves with the chief ointments: but they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph. 7 Therefore now shall they go captive with the first that go captive, and the banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed.

6.0.1.en: "Woe to them that are at ease in Zion, and trust in the mountain of Samaria, which are named chief of the nations, to whom the house of Israel came!" [1].

6.0.2.en: He pronounces the woe perhaps upon the great men, the nobles, and all who held religious and civil leadership in Judah and Israel, for they had become secure and settled down in Zion and Samaria, in a life of luxury and pampering, especially since they were counted as chief of the nations, that is, they were more exalted and honored than all the nations, or they were the firstfruits of the nations.

6.0.3.en: Zion was known for its towers and bulwarks, as the Psalmist says: "Walk about Zion, and go round about her: tell the towers thereof. Mark ye well her bulwarks, consider her palaces; that ye may tell it to the generation following" (Ps 48:12-13); it contained within it the thrones of the house of David (Ps 122:5). As for the mountain of Samaria, it had become the center of religious life for the northern kingdom. The great men in both regions lounged in security, since civil power and religious leadership were in their hands; the nations feared them and the house of Israel came to them.

6.0.4.en: This is the state of the soul that finds for itself a refuge other than God: it feels secure because of its temporal success or its religious reputation; everyone looks at it with honor and admiration, and in foolishness it settles down and rests secure, instead of continual striving and growth in the Lord.

6.0.5.en: To rouse the people of Zion and the mountain of Samaria to repentance, the Lord gave them examples of great cities that had borne a reputation for a long time and had perished. He mentioned Calneh, which Nimrod built in the land of Shinar (Gen 10:10) and which was utterly ruined; Hamath in Syria, whose gods Sennacherib boasted that he had destroyed (2 Kgs 18:34); and Gath in Philistia, which Hazael had ruined a short time before (2 Kgs 12:17)... Are Zion and the mountain of Samaria better than these cities, or is their border greater than their border?

6.0.6.en: Truly, it is fitting that we take warning from what happens to others. If sin has shattered giants, and negligence has ruined kingdoms, it is fitting for us not to accept sin and not to walk in laxity, lest we become an example and a warning like the others!

6.1.0.en: Israel did not take warning from what befell the kingdoms around it, and paid no heed to God's threats to it, absorbed in its injustice even in the courts of justice, supposing that chastisement would not come upon it soon. "Ye that put far away the evil day (the chastisement), and cause the seat of violence to come near" [3].

6.1.1.en: This life, marked by settling into evil and injustice and by indifference to God's warnings, was supported by their luxurious and pampered life, for their hearts were drawn into pleasures and lusts. God rebukes them, saying:

6.2.0.en: "That lie upon beds of ivory, and stretch themselves upon their couches, and eat the lambs out of the flock, and the calves out of the midst of the stall (the manger)" [4].

6.2.1.en: Their life was marked by sleep and slackness; they spent their time lying on beds inlaid with ivory and stretched out on their couches, eating many of the lambs and the fatted calves... People who know nothing of spiritual striving and seriousness: instead of the sackcloth that they ought to have girded themselves with because of their sins, they stretched themselves on beds all the days of their life, and instead of fasting and humility they eat greedily. As the Apostle Paul says of some wicked teachers: "For they that are such serve not our Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly" (Rom 16:18). And in another place he says: "Whose end is destruction, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who mind earthly things. For our conversation is in heaven" (Phil 3:19-20).

6.3.0.en: Thus they live for their bellies and walk as men of the dust seeking temporal pleasures, and instead of enjoying the divine heavenly praises they love a life of excessive revelry, offering corrupting songs bound up with licentious music which is the work of their own hands, whereas David offered his psalms in order to draw his heart to heaven: "That chant to the sound of the viol, and invent to themselves instruments of musick, like David" [5]. Perhaps in the time of their revelry they sang some religious songs, not for repentance but in mockery, as the people of Babylon asked the people of Israel to sing the songs of Zion in the land of captivity, and they answered: "How shall we sing the LORD's song in a strange land?" [4]. But these sang the songs of the Lord amid their revelry and drunkenness, in an atmosphere foreign to the Lord!

6.4.0.en: Pampering dominated their whole life: in their sleep, their eating, their revelry, and also in their drunkenness and their perfuming themselves with costly ointments: "That drink wine in bowls - basins, which are large bowls used for sacrificial purposes (Ex 38:3; Zech 14:20) - and anoint themselves with the chief ointments" [6].

6.4.1.en: St. Clement of Alexandria comments on these prophetic expressions, saying: [When the Holy Spirit spoke through Amos, He declared the wretchedness of the rich because of their luxurious life.] Tertullian says likewise: [Truly, (the rich) have found their consolation, their glory, their honor and the height of their position in their riches. And in Psalm 48 He turns us away from concern for these things, saying: "Be not thou afraid when one is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased; for when he dieth he shall carry nothing away: his glory shall not descend after him" (Ps 49:16-17), and in (Psalm 62) He says: "Do not desire riches, and if riches increase, set not your heart upon them" (Ps 62:10). Finally, this woe was pronounced by the prophet against the rich man who is attached to delights.] And St. John Chrysostom says: [Behold how God blames luxury also, for He does not condemn them here for greed they had committed but merely for extravagance. Here you are eating to the point of gluttony while Christ does not have what is necessary. You eat various cakes while Christ does not have dry bread. You drink Thasian wine and do not give Christ a cup of cold water, though He is thirsty. You lie on a soft embroidered bed while He perishes from cold!]

6.4.2.en: The Lord completes His description of this slack, pampered company by saying: "But they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph" [6]. This is the sin with which He closes His description of this company in order to pass judgment on it: "Therefore now shall they go captive with the first that go captive, and the banquet of them that stretched themselves shall be removed" [7]. What is this sin with which He concludes, so that He reckons them worthy to be the first of the captives and the feasts they used to spread and stretch themselves upon to be taken away from them?

6.4.3.en: "Joseph" most often refers to Israel as a whole, as though the heart of these slack great men had withdrawn into luxury and revelry, far from the affliction that Israel was passing through, like the person who in his luxury forgets the sufferings and sorrows of the Church.

6.4.4.en: Perhaps "the affliction of Joseph" reminds us of the chief butler who returned to his work and stood before Pharaoh, and forgot Joseph in prison (Gen 40:21, 23). So when a person lives in comfort and ease, he forgets his suffering and deprived brethren... It is a hideous picture that reveals man's selfishness and his cutting himself off from his membership in the holy congregation.

6.4.5.en: Many of the Fathers link this expression "they are not grieved for the affliction of Joseph" with what is written in the book of Micah (Mic 1:11): "She who dwells in Zaanan does not go forth to mourn over the place next to her" (Septuagint), saying that what befell Israel (Joseph) and the neighbors of Zaanan came by God's permission to chastise them, and yet, since we do not share their sorrow, this is counted as sin against us. As St. John Chrysostom says: [Even if they are being chastised justly, it is not fitting for you to rejoice at their harm... for God wants you to show compassion even on these. For if we, who are evil, when we punish a servant and see his fellow servant laughing, are all the more enraged and pour out our anger on the fellow servant (for his laughter), how much more will God punish those who are arrogant toward the one who is chastising them?] He also says: [Even if they are justly punished, God wants us to console them and not to rejoice or revile them. He says: "If I punish, I take no pleasure in it; I take no pleasure in the punishment of the sinner, since I do not desire his death" (Ezek 18:32). So it is fitting for you to imitate your Lord, and to grieve that the sinner has fallen under a just punishment, for whoever acquires such a good sorrow gathers great profit.]

6.5.0.en: 8 The Lord GOD hath sworn by himself, saith the LORD the God of hosts, "I abhor the excellency of Jacob, and hate his palaces: therefore will I deliver up the city with all that is therein." 9 And it shall come to pass, if there remain ten men in one house, that they shall die. 10 And a man's uncle shall take him up, and he that burneth him, to bring out the bones out of the house, and shall say unto him that is by the sides of the house, "Is there yet any with thee?" and he shall say, "No." Then shall he say, "Hold thy tongue: for we may not make mention of the name of the LORD." 11 For, behold, the LORD commandeth, and he will smite the great house with breaches, and the little house with clefts.

6.5.1.en: God pronounces woe upon Israel because it fell into pride, saying: "I abhor the excellency of Jacob, and hate his palaces: therefore will I deliver up the city with all that is therein" [8]. The city that He loves and upon which His name was called, He delivers up with its palaces and all that fills it, because of its vain greatness and boasting. He abhors it and delivers it to chastisement with an oath, so that all may be certain that the judgment will not be revoked.

6.5.2.en: St. John Climacus says of pride: [Pride is a denial of God, an invention of the demons, a contempt for men, a mother of condemnation, a daughter of praises, a sign of barrenness, a flight from God's help, a forerunner of madness of mind, a promoter of falls, a cause of epilepsy, a fountain of anger, a gate of hypocrisy, a helper of demons, a guardian of sins, a patroness of hardness of heart, an ignorance of compassion, a bitter accountant and an unjust judge, an adversary of God and the root of blasphemy,] and he also says: [Wherever a fall has come, there pride has gone before and dwelt, for the presence of the one announces the coming of the other.]

6.5.3.en: Since they fell into deadly pride, He pursued them with successive chastisements, until if only ten men remained in one house they would die. He presented a bitter picture of their state: the uncle carries the body of his brother's daughter, though one would expect a man to carry the body of his father and his uncle, and offers a burning for the dead as an honor to him (Jer 34:5; 2 Chr 16:14; 21:19), and when he asks who is in the house he finds that all have died, so that hearts rage against the Lord (Prov 19:3) and do not mention His name. Thus the ruin reaches the houses of Israel until there is no one to mention the name of the Lord. And the strange thing is that the Lord smites the great house with destruction and the little house so that it becomes clefts; He shatters the great before the small, and more violently, because of his increasing pride!

6.6.0.en: 12 Shall horses run upon the rock? will one plow there with oxen? for ye have turned judgment into gall, and the fruit of righteousness into hemlock: 13 Ye which rejoice in a thing of nought, which say, "Have we not taken to us horns by our own strength?" 14 "But, behold, I will raise up against you a nation, O house of Israel, saith the LORD the God of hosts; and they shall afflict you from the entering in of Hemath unto the river of the wilderness."

6.7.0.en: The third reason for their falling under the woes is: "Ye which rejoice in a thing of nought, which say, Have we not taken to us horns by our own strength?" [13]. They rejoice amid their pampering and luxury as though nothing would befall them, or as though what is said to them by way of warnings were vain words, relying on themselves and their strength... And this is the secret of their failure, for they close against themselves every way of escape, as He says: "Shall horses run upon the rock? will one plow there with oxen? for ye have turned judgment into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood" [12]. It is as though He says to them: I sent the prophets to you carrying warnings for your repentance and your return to me, and they found your hearts rock, upon which horses cannot run, nor oxen plow. You have turned judgment into poison and bitterness! You have made truth and righteousness lose their taste and benefit! Therefore He concludes His sermon by sending a nation to afflict them from every side: from the north "the entering in of Hemath," and from the south "the river of the wilderness" (the Arabah), which is a valley south of the Dead Sea as far as the Gulf of Aqaba...

7.0.0.en: 1 Thus hath the Lord GOD shewed unto me; and, behold, he formed grasshoppers in the beginning of the shooting up of the latter growth; and, lo, it was the latter growth after the king's mowings. 2 And it came to pass, that when they had made an end of eating the grass of the land, then I said, "O Lord GOD, forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small." 3 The LORD repented for this: "It shall not be," saith the LORD.

7.1.0.en: God had already threatened Israel through the prophet Amos that He would send locusts to eat their gardens, their vineyards, their fig trees and their olive trees (Amos 4:9), and now He showed him His plan, which was mingled with justice and mercy together; while He chastises, He was showing tenderness, and while He plans, He awaits a word of intercession from the prophet so that He may stop the chastisement [3].

7.1.1.en: He sent locusts that He Himself had prepared [1], for He entrusts no one with the chastisement of His children; even if He uses locusts or enemies, the hand of God remains the One who directs, and His eyes are upon them, like the potter who attends to the vessels he has placed in the furnace for a time. He prepared the locusts, but in their stage as larvae (at the beginning of the shooting up) [1], and they appeared after the king's mowings (that is, after the first harvest which was given as tribute to the king). He did not allow the locusts to eat the crop before the first harvest so that they might live on what they had already reaped as tribute to the king and not perish of hunger. It is as though, while He chastises, He does not permit destruction; so He let them reap the first harvest, and then destroyed the harvest with the locusts. As the Psalmist says: "O forsake me not utterly" (Ps 119:8), or "do not forsake me for long"; for in chastisement God seems to have forsaken us, but only until we return to Him, and then He returns to us.

7.1.2.en: The prophet interceded for Israel in humility, saying: "O Lord GOD, forgive, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small" [2]. This is the Jacob of whom God said, "I abhor the excellency of Jacob, and hate his palaces" (Amos 6:8). As soon as the prophet interceded for him, saying that he is small and cannot bear the chastisement, the Lord repented and stopped, not in the sense of changing His mind concerning him but in the sense of changing the situation itself.

7.1.3.en: Even in the bitterest moments of our chastisement, God longs to hear the voice of Amos in us interceding before Him in a spirit of humility, declaring that we are small and in need of Him, so that He lifts His chastisement and embraces us.

7.1.4.en: Some scholars see that the locust campaign was one of the attacks against Israel, whether stirred up by Aram or Assyria or others.

7.2.s.en: 2. The vision of the destroying fire:

7.2.0.en: 4 Thus hath the Lord GOD shewed unto me: and, behold, the Lord GOD called to contend by fire, and it devoured the great deep, and did eat up a part. 5 Then said I, "O Lord GOD, cease, I beseech thee: by whom shall Jacob arise? for he is small." 6 The LORD repented for this: "This also shall not be," saith the Lord GOD.

7.2.1.en: The first time God chastised with extreme tenderness, and since Israel did not turn back from its sin to God, He returned to chastise more severely; this time He does not chastise them in a hidden way but openly: "The Lord GOD called to contend by fire" [4]. As was said by the prophet Isaiah: "For, behold, the LORD will come with fire, and with his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his anger with fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire. For by fire and by his sword will the LORD plead with all flesh: and the slain of the LORD shall be many" (Isa 66:15-16), as he also said: "The LORD standeth up to plead, and standeth to judge the people" (Isa 3:13), and also: "Wherefore I will yet plead with you, saith the LORD, and with your children's children will I plead" (Jer 2:9), "For the LORD hath a controversy with the inhabitants of the land" (Hos 4:1).

7.2.2.en: God calls to an open trial not in order to take vengeance by our human understanding, but in order to turn the wicked from his wickedness by the fire of chastisement, burning up his sins, so that he returns to Him and enjoys His divine love.

7.2.3.en: In the first chastisement He was content with part of the harvest, but this time, as He chastises more firmly, He deprives them of water and food: the fire devours the great deep and the field, so that a person feels the need for One who will water him and satisfy him... and finds in God his drink and his food.

7.2.4.en: This time also God awaits the intercession of His prophet in order to forgive His people.

7.3.0.en: 7 Thus he shewed me: and, behold, the Lord stood upon a wall made by a plumbline, with a plumbline in his hand. 8 And the LORD said unto me, "Amos, what seest thou?" And I said, "A plumbline." Then said the Lord, "Behold, I will set a plumbline in the midst of my people Israel: I will not again pass by them any more: 9 And the high places of Isaac shall be desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste; and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword."

7.4.0.en: The Lord stood before the wall with the plumbline (a measure by which the straightness of a wall is known); God measured the kingdom of Israel with His divine plumbline and said: "I will not again pass by them any more" [8].

7.4.1.en: It was fitting for the Jewish Church to be a wall of faith in the Messiah, but she rejected this work and denied her Savior... This is what God's plumbline revealed, and so she deserved to be torn down. So too souls that receive a spiritual leadership task, if they are not faithful and do not walk as a wall for others supporting them in their spiritual striving, deserve to be torn down.

7.4.2.en: The Lord says through Isaiah: "Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet" (Isa 28:17), and the prophet David measured the Moabites with a line, to put to death and with one full line to keep alive (1 Sam 8:2), and when Manasseh king of Judah did evil, the Lord said: "And I will stretch over Jerusalem the line of Samaria, and the plummet of the house of Ahab: and I will wipe Jerusalem as a man wipeth a dish, wiping it, and turning it upside down" (2 Kgs 21:13).

7.4.3.en: Perhaps His use of the plumbline means that He offers His divine chastisements by measure, with great precision, according to what we can bear and according to our need for building up, although it is preceded by the tearing down of what is crooked in us.

7.5.0.en: The prophet continues his speech: "And the high places of Isaac shall be desolate, and the sanctuaries of Israel shall be laid waste; and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword" [9]. What does he mean by this destruction? If they take refuge in the high places and reckon that the sanctuaries fortify them and that their present king is strong, then their high places become a wasteland, their sanctuaries a ruin, and their king Jeroboam with all his house are given over to slaughter.

7.5.1.en: In the age of the patriarchs the high places were considered the best place for setting up altars and offering sacrifices to the Lord, perhaps because they are elevated... as though man in his relation with God rises above earthly and temporal things. But the Jews' mixing with the Gentiles led them to set up idolatrous altars on the high places, so the prophets rose up attacking the high places as a symbol of idolatry, especially since the Lord now had His temple in Jerusalem, and it was not permitted to offer sacrifices outside it.

7.5.2.en: Perhaps He chose "the high places of Isaac" because "Isaac" means (laughter), as though they would become a laughingstock and a mockery among the nations because of the destruction that befalls them.

7.5.3.en: As for the sword that rises against the house of Jeroboam the Second, it is the sword of Assyria.

7.6.0.en: 10 Then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, "Amos hath conspired against thee in the midst of the house of Israel: the land is not able to bear all his words. 11 For thus Amos saith, Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely be led away captive out of their own land."

7.6.1.en: Instead of Israel, with its king, its leaders, its priests and its people, offering repentance, as the people of Nineveh did when they heard the prophet Jonah rebuking them, the priest of Bethel informs against the prophet Amos to King Jeroboam the Second, saying: "Amos hath conspired against thee in the midst of the house of Israel: the land is not able to bear all his words. For thus Amos saith, Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely be led away captive out of their own land" [10-11].

7.6.2.en: Instead of Amaziah doing his work as a priest proclaiming the truth, he turns the truth into wormwood; he made of Amos's prophecies a conspiracy against the king in the midst of the people, and counted the prophet's words not a message of repentance and the building up of the community but an agitation of the people against the king and his men! The priest's heart had turned away from service to temporal positions, earthly glory and love of the world, so it is no wonder that he distorts the prophet's message and disfigures the divine work, as though it were a work against the king and the people... as though it were national treason!

7.6.3.en: He says to the king, "the land is not able to bear all his words," suggesting to the king that the whole people are against Amos and that his preaching is intolerable to everyone. These are the words of the enemy of good in every age, as he suggests to people that God's words are unacceptable and preaching the Gospel is intolerable and unrealistic, in order to turn them aside from God's work and take them outside the circle of the Cross.

7.6.4.en: He says "the land is not able to bear all his words"... Truly, the priest Amaziah was earth and not heaven, and could not bear the prophet's words. The carnal man is a man of dust who walks with an earthly mind, so he does not accept what belongs to God and cannot endure the heavenly life; therefore "the land is not able to bear all his words."

7.6.5.en: When the Lord Christ spoke of His holy Body and Blood, given as the secret of eternal life, many of His disciples said: "This is an hard saying; who can hear it?... From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him" (Jn 6:60, 66).

7.7.0.en: "12 Also Amaziah said unto Amos, 'O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: 13 But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court.'" [12-13].

7.7.1.en: Amaziah supposed of Amos that he was a prophet in order to eat bread, but Amos was not so; he prophesies not as a job to live from, but because he is an instrument in the hand of God his Creator. It is no wonder that the priest drives out the prophet, for the latter, despite his simplicity, by his faithfulness and courage uncovers the secret of the former and exposes his life.

7.7.2.en: St. Jerome says: [Amos was driven out of Samaria. Why? Surely because here, as in other cases, he is a spiritual surgeon who cuts off the members infected with sin, and urges the people to repentance. The Apostle Paul says: "Am I therefore become your enemy, because I tell you the truth?" (Gal 4:16)].

7.7.3.en: Amos was not an official prophet from the school of the prophets, who acquired prophecy by learning or inheritance... but he was faithful in the eyes of God, better than the holder of official authority, the priest of Bethel. Therefore St. Jerome says in one of his letters: [Not all bishops are truly bishops. You look at Peter; observe Judas also. You look at Stephen; see Nicodemus, who was condemned in the Apocalypse by the very lips of the Lord (Amos 2:6), who raised up the heresy of the Nicolaitans through his imaginations. Therefore "let a man examine himself" (1 Cor 11:28) and come; it is not ecclesiastical rank that makes him a Christian!]

7.8.0.en: 14 Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: 15 And the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel. 16 Now therefore hear thou the word of the LORD: Thou sayest, Prophesy not against Israel, and drop not thy word against the house of Isaac. 17 Therefore thus saith the LORD; Thy wife shall be an harlot in the city, and thy sons and thy daughters shall fall by the sword, and thy land shall be divided by line; and thou shalt die in a polluted land: and Israel shall surely go into captivity forth of his land."

7.8.1.en: In humility filled with courage Amos said to Amaziah: "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: and the LORD took me as I followed the flock, and the LORD said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel" [14-15].

7.8.2.en: In humility he did not deny his former lowly work as a shepherd of sheep and a gatherer of sycamore fruit, and in courage he declared that it was the Lord who called him from behind the sheep to prophesy to God's people Israel... He is not a prophet in the minds of some, because he was not trained in the school of the prophets and did not inherit prophecy, so he is not a son of a prophet, but he is a prophet by a personal call from God, and so he is bound to do the work given by the One who called him.

7.8.3.en: St. John Chrysostom says: [He did not say this to boast of himself (that God called him to prophecy), but to silence the mouths of those who supposed that he was not a prophet, showing them that he is not a deceiver and does not speak anything of his own accord.]

7.8.4.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus speaks of the Holy Spirit who worked in Amos to raise him up as a prophet, saying: [This Spirit, being all-wise and all-loving, when He takes possession of a shepherd makes him a psalmist who drives away evil spirits with his psalm (1 Sam 16:23), and when He acquires a shepherd of sheep and gatherer of sycamore fruit makes him a prophet. Remember David and Amos!]

7.8.5.en: Finally, in boldness the prophet Amos did not keep silent but declared to him that his wife would be a harlot, his sons and daughters would fall by the sword, his land would be divided by line, and he himself would die in a polluted land and Israel would be led away captive from its land. Perhaps this was fulfilled literally at the captivity of Israel by Assyria, when one of the attacking soldiers committed evil with Amaziah's wife, and he lost his sons and daughters, while he was carried to an idolatrous land to die there.

7.8.6.en: How bitter it is when the priest of the Lord or his son becomes corrupt, so that the Lord abandons him to corrupt his body like Amaziah's wife who committed adultery, and he loses his gifts and abilities, which are scattered like Amaziah's sons and daughters slain by the sword, and instead of inheriting he loses what he has, so that strangers divide his land and he falls into disgrace, and because of him also the Church is led captive, as many fall and stumble!
